title: Basics
body: Basics Getting started MarkText is a realtime preview editor for markdown with various markdown extensions. You can simply write and edit text and MarkText hides all unnecessary syntax elements. You can see key bindings or command palette ( CmdOrCtrl + Shift + P ) for all available commands or start a new line and type to get an overlay with available text elements. MarkText provides a minimal and simple interface and in the next sections you can learn more about the interface and features. Interface Toggle sidebar Toggle the sidebar with CmdOrCtrl + J . It contains the filesystem explorer and find-in-files search. The file tree also has a collapsible _Opened Files_ section, controlled by the preference. The document outline is independent of the sidebar. Use or CmdOrCtrl + K to expand or collapse it. On narrow windows it appears as a floating panel; a document needs headings for the outline to appear. Toggle tabs MarkText can be used as a single editor but opens all files in a separate tab. Tabs can be shown or hidden through the View menu and reordered by drag and drop. The shortcut is Option + Command + B on macOS and Ctrl + Shift + B on Linux and Windows. Want to use tabs without showing them?** You can hide tabs and use key bindings such as Ctrl + Tab to cycle through tabs or the sidebar _opened files_ panel. Switch between editor modes Use the View menu to switch between the WYSIWYG and source-code editor. The shortcut is Option + Command + S on macOS and Ctrl + E on Linux and Windows. The realtime preview editor is the default editor with many features. A detailed overview of all features can be found here. Typewriter and focus mode Use CmdOrCtrl + Shift + J for focus mode. Typewriter mode uses Option + Command + T on macOS and Ctrl + Shift + G on Linux and Windows. :smile_cat:Edit modes:dog: Source Code | Typewriter | Focus | :-----------------------: | :---------------------------: | :----------------------: | | | | Open and modify markdown files Open your first file You can use the menu or press CmdOrCtrl + O to open a file dialog to choose a markdown file. Another way to is to launch MarkText with directories or files via command line. Save your edited file After some modifications you can save your file via CmdOrCtrl + S or use _save as_ to use a different file name. Open a directory MarkText also has support to open a directory via CmdOrCtrl + Shift + O through the File menu. After opening a directory, the sidebar tree shows supported files and directories, subject to watcher exclusions. The tree view allows you to open further files, browse and modify files or directories inside the opened root directory. Opened files appear in a separate section above the folder tree. You can also use quick open ( CmdOrCtrl + P ) to quickly open a file from the opened root directory or editor and navigate via arrow keys or select a file via mouse. Use the sidebar search control to find text in files. Preview tabs Since 0.23.0, single-clicking a sid

title: Editing in depth
body: Editing in Depth Let us take a look at the realtime editor and editing features. Text manipulation MarkText shows you formatted text in realtime, where you can simply write and edit text, as well as use markdown syntax. To improve your writing efficiency there are a lot of key bindings for better text manipulation. In the preferences you can control the editor settings such as font settings, autocompletion and line width. Selections You can select text with your mouse cursor, double click on a word or use the keyboard Shift + Arrow Keys . Format overlay:** The format overlay is a pop-up that automatically appears when you're selecting text. You can easily transform text and inline markdown, and remove formatting. Bold Italics Underline Strikethrough Highlight (when enabled in Markdown preferences) Text and background colors Inline code Inline math formulas Create link Create image Remove formatting Further overlays are available for emojis, links, images and tables. Deleting Do you want to delete headings, lists or tables? Just select the area and press backspace. Brackets and quotes autocompletion You can configure MarkText to autocomplete markdown syntax, brackets and quotes. These options are enabled by default. Pair insertion depends on the cursor context, such as surrounding characters and whether the cursor is inside code or math. Links Links are displayed by default as normal text, but if you click on a link it is shown as a markdown link with title and URL, as shown below: Formatting MarkText parses and exports Markdown using Muya, with CommonMark/GFM syntax and optional extensions controlled by preferences. Some settings, such as list indentation, can be controlled via preferences. Editing features Quick insert When you start a new line, just type / to access a pop-up with all available markdown features. At this point, you can choose an entry and the line is transformed into the selected attribute. Line transformer You can transform a line into another type by clicking on the highlighted icon in the image below and select . Furthermore, you can duplicate the selected line, create a paragraph after the selected block or delete the line. Table tools It's sometimes hard to write and manage tables in markdown. In MarkText you can press CmdOrCtrl + Shift + T to get a table dialog and create a table with variable row and column count. Both row and column count can be changed via the table tools (first icon above the table) later if necessary. You can apply inline formatting in a table cell and align the text via table tools at the top of the table. Insert and delete rows and columns:** You can insert or delete a new row or column by clicking on an existing cell and clicking on the menu on the right side for rows or bottom for columns. Move table cells:** You can simply move a row or column by clicking on the cell menu (like above) and dragging it by holding your left mouse button like this: Image tools MarkText provides an image viewer and a

title: Spelling
body: Spelling MarkText can automatically check your text for misspelled words as you type and suggest corrections. You just need to enable spell checking in settings under *spelling* to never miss a misspelled word. We're using Hunspell for Linux and older Windows versions and on macOS and Window 10 you can choose between Hunspell or the system spell checker (default). You can control the default proofing language via settings but can change the language at runtime via right-click menu entry under without changing the default language. By default MarkText only support American English for Hunspell and the local available languages for the system spell checker. You can download 42 languages for Hunspell and many more for macOS and Windows 10 via system settings. Features Automatic language detection:** MarkText can try to automatically detect the language while typing and we're currently support over 160 languages by Compact Language Detector. Don't underline misspelled words:** If you don't like that all spelling mistakes are red highlighted, you can disable this feature in settings but still benefit from manually spell checking via right-click menu. Disabling constantly spell checking will also improve performance overall. Adding words to dictionary:** You can add words to the selected dictionary by right-clicking on a misspelled word and select or remove a previously added word. If you want to temporary ignore a word, select . Manage dictionaries macOS spell checker You need to add the additional language dictionaries via *"Language & Region"* in your system preferences pane. Windows spell checker On Windows 10, you need to add additional language dictionaries via *"Language"* in your *"Time & language"* settings. Add the additional language(s) and download the *"Basic typing"* language option for each language. Hunspell Please go to spelling settings and scroll to the bottom. Now you see a list of available language dictionaries and can add additional dictionaries via the drop-down menu at the bottom. Please note that an active internet connection is required to download a dictionary!

title: Markdown syntax
body: Markdown Syntax This guide introduces Markdown syntax supported by MarkText and the optional extensions controlled by Preferences → Markdown. Contents** CommonMark - Headings - Paragraphs - Breaks - Horizontal Rule - Emphasis - Links - Images - Blockquotes - Lists - Code - Raw HTML - Escaping with backslashes GitHub Flavored Markdown - Strikethrough - Todo List - Tables - Extended autolinks Pandoc Extension - Footnotes - Superscript and subscript - Math Formulas Others - GitHub Alerts - Highlight - Inline diff - Multiline blockquote - Keyboard Keys - Emojis - Front Matter - Named Anchors - Syntax highlighting - Diagrams Credits CommonMark The base syntax below is defined by CommonMark. Headings ATX headings use one to six characters followed by a space: Setext headings use an underline: for level 1 or for level 2. Paragraphs Just write normal text: Breaks A blank line separates paragraphs. Multiple blank lines do not guarantee extra visual spacing. Two trailing spaces or a backslash at the end of a line create a hard line break: A single newline within a paragraph is a soft line break. MarkText's preference controls whether it displays as a space or a line break. Horizontal Rule The HTML element is for creating a "thematic break" between paragraph-level elements. In markdown, you can use of the following for this purpose: : three consecutive underscores : three consecutive dashes : three consecutive asterisks Renders to: Emphasis Bold For emphasizing a snippet of text with a heavier font-weight. The following snippet of text is **rendered as bold text**. renders to: rendered as bold text** Italics For emphasizing a snippet of text with italics. The following snippet of text is _rendered as italicized text_. renders to: rendered as italicized text_ Links Autolinks Autolinks are absolute URIs and email addresses inside and . They are parsed as links, where the URI or email address itself is used as the link's label. Renders to: Blockquotes Used for defining a section of quoting text from another source, within your document. To create a blockquote, use before any text you want to quote. Renders to: Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. Integer posuere erat a ante. Blockquotes can also be nested: Renders to: Donec massa lacus, ultricies a ullamcorper in, fermentum sed augue. Nunc augue augue, aliquam non hendrerit ac, commodo vel nisi. > Sed adipiscing elit vitae augue consectetur a gravida nunc vehicula. Donec auctor > odio non est accumsan facilisis. Aliquam id turpis in dolor tincidunt mollis ac eu diam. > > > Donec massa lacus, ultricies a ullamcorper in, fermentum sed augue. > > Nunc augue augue, aliquam non hendrerit ac, commodo vel nisi. Lists Unordered A list of items in which the order of the items does not explicitly matter. You may use any of the following symbols to denote bullets for each list item: For example Renders to: Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet Consectetur adipiscing elit Integer molestie lorem at massa Facilisis

headings.text: Making marktext available in your shell

body: Command Line Interface Opening files in read-only mode Pass before or after the files to open every file from that command in the editor's Reading Mode: The option applies only to the files supplied to that invocation. It does not change the default open mode for later files, and you can switch a document back to Edit Mode from the View menu when needed. A missing file is reported as an error instead of being created as an empty read-only buffer. Making available in your shell has to point at your installation of MarkText. Where that is — and what you have to do about it — varies from platform to platform. Linux The and packages already install , and the Snap exposes a command, so there is nothing to set up. For the AppImage or the tarball, alias the binary you extracted: macOS Windows Add the installation directory to your — for a default install — or save a wrapper like this one as in a directory that is already on it: Do **not** put a symlink, a hard link or a lone copy of on your . Chromium looks for and the other bundled resources in the directory of the executable path it was launched from, and Windows reports the link's own path rather than the target's. MarkText then aborts before it starts, printing only: Linking is safe on Linux — from the and packages is itself a symlink into — because the kernel resolves the link before the process starts.

title: Export a document
body: Export a Document MarkText allows you to export a markdown document as PDF and HTML file or to print the document. Options Page options PDF and print exports provide page size, orientation and margin controls. HTML export instead provides a page-title field. Style Adjust the page style without modify the page theme: Overwrite font family, size and line height. Auto numbering headings. Option to show the front matter on the exported document. Theme MarkText allows you to select a page theme before exporting. You can learn more about page themes here. Header and footer You can include a header and/or footer in the exported document if you choose PDF or printing and also adjust the header/footer style. You can select between no, a single or a three cell header in export options. The header is repeated through the export page layout; the footer is fixed at the bottom. Footer cells are constrained to one line. The settings do not expose a page-number field. An example can be seen below. Markdown extensions and media The HTML/PDF renderer reads the document's math, footnote, superscript/subscript, highlight, inline-diff, multiline-blockquote and GitHub Alerts options. For example, enable GitHub Alerts in Preferences → Markdown to render alert blocks with their associated styling (since 0.22.0). Folded headings still export their full section contents. Exporting a diagram as PNG or SVG is a separate action in the media viewer, rather than a whole-document export format.

body: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) What are the supported platforms? MarkText is a desktop application and available for: Linux x64 and arm64 (arm64 release packages are available since 0.23.0) macOS 12 (Monterey) or later, x64 and arm64 (Apple Silicon) Windows x64 and arm64 The current Electron 42-based application requires macOS 12 or later. See the Electron announcement removing macOS 11 support. Is MarkText open-source and free? Yes, MarkText is licensed under the MIT license and completely free for everyone. The source-code is available on GitHub. Can I use MarkText as note management/taking app? MarkText is a pure markdown editor without features such as knowledge management and tags but yes, you can do this via the integrated filesystem explorer and task lists. Where can I find documentation? The full documentation is available on the MarkText website: End-user documentation Developer documentation Can I run a portable version of MarkText? Yes, please see here for further information. How can I report bugs and problems? You can report bugs and problems via our GitHub issue tracker. Please provide a detailed description of the problem to better solve the issue. I cannot launch MarkText on Linux (SUID sandbox) If Chromium reports that its sandbox helper is not configured correctly, see the Linux notes. The cause and available remedies depend on the distribution, package format and system sandbox configuration.

title: Architecture
body: Project Architecture MarkText is an Electron application with a Vue 3 interface and a separate TypeScript editor engine, Muya. The desktop application, editor engine and website share a pnpm workspace. Repository layout Root desktop commands proxy to . Paths beginning with in the desktop developer guides are relative to unless stated otherwise. Electron boundaries Main process initializes the application. The main process has Node.js and Electron access and owns windows, filesystem operations, native dialogs, file watchers and operating-system integrations. Avoid blocking it with long synchronous operations. Preload bridge exposes typed APIs through . Editor and preferences windows both use , and in . Renderer code accesses capabilities through , , and other narrow bridge APIs. It cannot import Node.js or Electron directly. Main and preload compile to CommonJS; the renderer compiles to ES modules. Production windows enable web security. Development disables it to load document-local images from the Vite HTTP origin. Keep this development exception distinct from production behavior when debugging resources. Renderer mounts the Vue application for an editor window. Pinia stores coordinate tabs, document modes, preferences, layout and folder roots. Each window hosts the Muya WYSIWYG editor and a CodeMirror source editor. Source mode transfers Markdown between CodeMirror and Muya. Reading mode is tracked per document and protects editing and writes across the renderer and main process. The independent document outline derives from the active document's headings. Muya is the public entry point of . The engine handles Markdown parsing, block data, editing interactions, rendering and Markdown/HTML export without Electron APIs. It is consumed as a workspace dependency by the desktop app. At runtime, electron-vite and Vitest resolve the package's source through its map. Desktop type checking uses generated declarations in to keep the two packages' compiler settings separate. See TypeScript. Opening a document 1. A file-menu action or command requests a native open dialog in the main process. 2. The application selects an editor window, loads the document and registers filesystem watching. 3. The main process sends through IPC. 4. The renderer editor store creates or selects the document tab and notifies the editor host. 5. The active document is loaded into the appropriate editor view. Sidebar opens can reuse a preview tab. Editing the document or double-clicking the sidebar file keeps that tab open. Folder state is maintained separately: one window can host multiple roots, each with its own tree and watcher state; folder search covers available roots. See IPC for the communication contract, Interface for the window layout, and Build instructions for package-specific checks.

title: Interface
body: Interface Main interface Green: titlebar Orange: sidebar Red: editor with tabs and per-tab notification at the bottom The editor window contains a title bar, an optional sidebar, optional tabs and the document editor. A separate outline panel navigates the active document's headings. Layout visibility is coordinated by . Titlebar The title bar shows document information and the statistics counter. Linux and Windows expose the application menu and window controls in the custom title bar; the preference also offers native window decorations. macOS uses the hidden-inset title-bar configuration in . Sidebar The optional, resizable sidebar contains the filesystem explorer and a find-in-files search powered by ripgrep. The explorer includes a collapsible _Opened Files_ section ( ). In the 0.24.0 development version, it supports multiple folder roots, search across available roots, and a draggable divider below Opened Files. The document outline is a separate responsive panel, available since 0.23.0. It lists the active document's headings and can remain expanded or float in a compact window. The title-bar statistics popover shows document and selection counts, file timestamps and a per-tab Reading Mode switch. Editor The editor is the core element that hosts the realtime preview editor called Muya and consists of three parts. Tabs are located at the top and at the bottom the per-tab notification bar is located for events like file changed or deleted. The main part is the editor that is either provided by Muya or CodeMirror for the source-code editor. There are multiple overlays available like inline toolbar, emoji picker, quick insert or image tools. Hovering a rendered diagram, math block or HTML block shows a small toolbar in its top-right corner; for a diagram it also offers a view action that opens the diagram full-screen in the media viewer, which is shared with the image preview and adds zoom, pan and image export.

title: Release process

headings.text: 1. Cut a release branch (first RC only)

body: Releasing MarkText The release pipeline is triggered by pushing a tag. The workflow ( ) then runs **validate → build (6-platform matrix) → publish** and creates a GitHub Release with installers and . Release notes explicitly compare against the highest published stable version below the new version, selected from all release pages by . Drafts, prereleases, and the current version are excluded. RCs compare against the previous stable cycle; hotfixes exclude newer versions. For example, compares against even if that tag is on a separate release branch. The workflow fails if no earlier stable release exists instead of falling back to GitHub's automatic comparison base. Verify the link during release review. The flow below covers both release candidates and stable releases — same steps, only the version string differs. Prerequisites Push access to CLI authenticated ( ) A clean checkout of the latest 1. Cut a release branch (first RC only) Reuse the same branch for every RC of that minor version ( , , …) **and** the eventual stable tag. For follow-ups, just and skip to step 2. 2. Bump the application version Set the same in the root and . The desktop package determines the installer and application version. Muya and the website keep their independent package versions. Update with the release highlights. Check lockfile consistency with , then run lint, typecheck, unit tests, build, and relevant E2E tests before pushing the release tag. Stage | Version string | ----------------- | ------------------------------- | Release candidate | , , … | Stable | | 3. Commit and push the branch 4. Tag and push A tag push automatically publishes a public release after all builds succeed; it does not stop at a draft. Confirm the release commit and required CI checks before pushing. A in the tag (e.g. ) tells the workflow to mark the GitHub Release as **pre-release** automatically. Plain tags publish as stable releases. 5. Open a tracking PR (RC only) Open a **draft** PR from → for visibility. Do **not** merge it until the matching stable tag is pushed — merging an RC commit would freeze at the RC version. 6. Monitor the workflow Approximate timing: validate ~30 s · build matrix ~15–30 min (6 platforms in parallel) · publish ~1 min. 7. Verify the published release Confirm: badge on the release page (RC only) **29 assets**: - **Linux x64** (5): , , , , - **Linux arm64** (4): , , , - **macOS arm64** (4): , , , - **macOS x64** (4): , , , - **Windows x64** (3): , , - **Windows arm64** (3): , , - **Auto-updater metadata** (5): , , , , - **Checksums** (1): Auto-generated release notes list the PRs merged since the previous tag 8. Post-stable cleanup (after stable ships) 1. Mark the tracking PR from step 5 ready for review and merge into 2. Open a follow-up PR bumping 's root and desktop files to the next dev version (e.g. ) For hotfixes off a previously-released tag, see RELEASE_HOTFIX.md. Once the hotfix branch is ready, steps 2–7 above apply.

title: Hotfix release
body: Prepare a Hotfix Start from the published tag that needs the fix, rather than from a development branch that may include unreleased features. Replace with the affected release tag and with the intended patch version. Apply the fix directly or cherry-pick the relevant commit: Resolve any conflicts and run the relevant checks and platform builds. Follow Releasing MarkText to update both application package versions, record release highlights, commit, tag and verify the published artifacts. The tag triggers public publication once the release workflow succeeds. Bring applicable fixes back to through a PR so later releases retain them.
